kp.k: Clone pitch prompts argument, not verified technical evidence
kp.d: Srivastava reports Mike's pitch that Harvey and Legora were rebuilt in two weeks using Claude and made open-source. She explicitly states that she has not tested the code, so the reported pitch is a trigger for her structural argument rather than a verified finding about the clone's capabilities.
qs: "I built Harvey and Legora in two weeks with Claude and made it open-source."
I haven't tested the code. I won't pretend I have.

kp.k: Interface-based legal AI moats face inevitable replication
kp.d: Srivastava argues that where a product's competitive moat consists of a user interface over an LLM, eventual replication is structurally inevitable. She frames legal AI vendors as racing open-source clones; this is a competitive-market thesis, not a measured finding about replication costs or vendor performance.
qs: But this is the structural inevitability worth paying attention to: when the moat is a UI on top of an LLM, someone will eventually rebuild it on a Saturday.
The vendors are racing the open-source clones.

kp.k: Lawyer-owned agents replace reliance on packaged products
kp.d: Srivastava predicts that the lawyers she characterises as those who matter in 2026 will use neither Harvey nor Mike, instead running their own agents configured to their workflows on Commercial Terms API. Her proposed direction for legal AI centres on ownership of workflows rather than selection of a vendor product or its open-source clone.
qs: The lawyers who matter in 2026 won't be on Harvey. They won't be on Mike either.
They'll be running their own agents, configured to their own workflow, on Commercial Terms API.
The future of legal AI isn't a product. It's a workflow you own.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Srivastava predicts that readily replicated legal-AI interfaces will give way to lawyer-owned, workflow-specific agents rather than dependence on branded products or their open-source clones.
pts.d: Srivastava argues that a vendor's competitive moat is vulnerable when it consists of a user interface on top of an LLM. She describes vendors as competing against open-source clones and predicts that the lawyers she calls those 'who matter' will use their own agents, configured to their workflows, on 'Commercial Terms API,' rather than Harvey or Mike. Her broader thesis is that ownership of workflows, rather than use of a particular legal-AI product, will define the future.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The thesis is prompted by Mike's promotional claim of rapid open-source replication; Srivastava explicitly says she has not tested its code.
pts.d: The document quotes Mike's pitch that Harvey and Legora were built in two weeks using Claude and made open-source. This is a third-party promotional assertion, not Srivastava's own development experience or a verified finding of equivalent functionality. Srivastava uses it to motivate a structural argument about replicability. She supplies no code testing, performance benchmarks, adoption data, or other empirical support for the predicted shift to lawyer-owned agents.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The lawyer-adoption prediction explicitly concerns 2026; replication is framed as eventual and conditional on a UI-over-LLM moat.
pts.d: Srivastava specifies 2026 for her prediction about influential lawyers using their own workflow-configured agents. Her 'eventually' and 'on a Saturday' language conveys the prospect of rapid replication without specifying a measured development time. The stated condition is that the vendor's moat is a UI on top of an LLM, rather than a demonstrated claim that every legal-AI product has only that moat. The wider workflow-ownership thesis has no separate deadline, while competition with clones is described as already occurring.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted changes concern lawyers choosing and configuring AI tools, legal-AI vendors facing replication, and open-source alternatives that may also be bypassed.
pts.d: Lawyers are depicted as moving from product users to operators of their own workflow-specific agents. Harvey is explicitly identified as a product these lawyers will not use; Mike is likewise predicted to be bypassed, so the claim is not simply that open-source products replace proprietary ones. Legal-AI vendors face competitive pressure from clones. Legora appears in the quoted replication pitch, not in a separate author prediction about its users. The source does not identify firm sizes, practice areas, client groups, staffing consequences, or public access-to-justice effects, and does not define which lawyers 'matter.'
